\chapter{Greetings and responses}
\label{ch:persian-greetings}
\hlchaptermodality{1}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can greet someone in Persian, respond courteously, answer yes or no, and copy one alef with a visible model.}

Hold a four-line greeting exchange, point to its right-to-left start, and copy one alef beside the visible model.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[salâm]{\fa{سلام} — hello, one joined word at a time}

\label{lesson:FA-C01-salam}



\begin{quote}
One greeting is enough for this lesson. Listen once: \textbf{salâm}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \fa{سلام}}
Persian runs \textbf{right to left}. Start at the right edge of \textbf{\fa{سلام}} and let your eyes travel towards the left while you say \emph{salâm}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{سلام}} — \emph{salâm} — hello
\end{quote}

Treat the joined word as one familiar greeting today. You do not need its four letter names, its joining rules, or the rest of the alphabet yet.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{salâm} means “hello” and literally evokes peace. Persian borrowed it from Arabic, where the consonants \textbf{s-l-m} organize a family concerned with peace, safety, and wholeness. That same old Semitic family also includes Hebrew \emph{shalom}. The word is now thoroughly everyday Persian.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Say \textbf{salâm} to one person or a group. It is neutral, friendly, and safe in most situations.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item See a neighbor: \textbf{Salâm!}
  \item Answer a greeting: \textbf{Salâm!}
\end{itemize}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Writing — follow one visible stroke}
Keep this model visible: \textbf{\fa{ا}}. With your finger, trace its one upright stroke from top to bottom. Do not copy it yet and do not hunt for it inside the joined word. The next two-minute lesson will name and copy this one shape.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Point to:} to the right edge, where Persian reading begins
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{salâm} once to greet, and once to answer
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which direction does Persian run? (\textbf{Right to left.}) What old idea lives inside \emph{salâm}? (\textbf{Peace, safety, or wholeness.}) Say the greeting once.

\href{https://sites.la.utexas.edu/persian\_online\_resources/the-writing-system/}{Persian Online: the writing system}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[alef]{\fa{ا} — one stroke with the model present}

\label{lesson:FA-W00-alef-guided-copy}



\begin{quote}
Point to the right edge of \textbf{\fa{سلام}} and say \emph{salâm}. Keep this separate one-stroke model visible: \textbf{\fa{ا}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — meet alef}
The shape is \textbf{\fa{ا}}, named \textbf{alef}. Draw its one straight stroke from top to bottom, then lift. In \emph{salâm}, alef carries the long \textbf{â} sound.

\subsection*{Writing — one guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\fa{ا}} once beside the model. Look back whenever you need. Say the long \emph{â} as your pen reaches the bottom, then stop.

Do not hide the model, copy the whole greeting, or add a second letter today. One visible stroke is enough for a first Persian writing lesson.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Compare your copy with \textbf{\fa{ا}}. How many strokes? (\textbf{One.}) Which way did that stroke travel? (\textbf{Top to bottom.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mamnun]{\fa{ممنون} — thank you}

\label{lesson:FA-C01-mamnoon}



\begin{quote}
One more expression, and the exchange starts to work: \emph{mamnun}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{ممنون}} — \emph{mamnun} — thank you
\end{quote}

Read it the way you read the greeting: from the right edge, as one whole word with its romanization beside it. One thing about the writing is worth noticing now, because it is true of nearly every Persian word you will meet: \textbf{the short vowels are not written}. The \emph{a} in \emph{mamnun} is part of the word you hear, not a mark you read. The letters themselves get their own lessons later; none is being asked of you today.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{mamnun} literally describes someone as \textbf{grateful or obliged}, and in ordinary conversation it simply works as “thanks.” Persian received it from Arabic, where the consonant family \textbf{m-n-n} gathers ideas of favour and kindness — the same kind of three-consonant family that gave you \emph{salâm}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Build the smallest exchange there is, and treat each expression as one social move rather than a sentence to analyse:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item A: \textbf{\fa{سلام}} — \emph{salâm} — Hello.
  \item B: \textbf{\fa{سلام}} — \emph{salâm} — Hello.
  \item A: \textbf{\fa{ممنون}} — \emph{mamnun} — Thank you.
\end{itemize}

No grammar is due. Two people, three moves.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{salâm} — \emph{mamnun}, the two moves in order
  \item what \emph{mamnun} literally describes — someone grateful or obliged
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \emph{salâm — mamnun} without looking. What does \emph{mamnun} literally describe? (\textbf{Someone grateful, or obliged to you.}) Which vowels does Persian writing leave out? (\textbf{The short ones.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bale]{\fa{بله} — yes}

\label{lesson:FA-C01-bale}



\begin{quote}
A greeting and a thank-you need an answer. Here is the polite one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{بله}} — \emph{bale} — yes
\end{quote}

Three letters, and \textbf{both} of its vowels are among the short ones Persian leaves out — so the written word carries no vowel at all and the reader supplies \emph{a} and \emph{e}. That is the same habit you just met in \emph{mamnun}, met twice in one short word. Read the romanization and take the shape as a whole; no letter is being asked of you yet.

\begin{culture}
\emph{bale} is the standard, polite “yes.” A more casual \emph{âre} exists, but one clear affirmative is plenty for now.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “Is this Persian?” — \emph{\textbf{Bale.}}
  \item “Are you ready?” — \emph{\textbf{Bale, mamnun.}} — Yes, thank you.
\end{itemize}
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bale}, once on its own
  \item \emph{bale, mamnun} — yes, thank you
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Answer “yes” in Persian once. (\emph{\textbf{Bale.}}) Which sounds does the writing leave for you to supply? (\textbf{The short vowels — here both of them.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[na]{\fa{نه} — no}

\label{lesson:FA-C01-na}



\begin{quote}
The other answer — and the smallest word in the chapter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{نه}} — \emph{na} — no
\end{quote}

Two letters and, once again, an unwritten short \emph{a}. The second of the two is the shape that also ends \emph{bale}, so part of this word is already familiar to your eye. Recognising a repeated shape is all that is asked; naming it is a later lesson's job.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{salâm} and \emph{mamnun} both arrived from Arabic. \emph{na} did not. It continues a very old \textbf{Indo-Iranian} negative, and relatives of it turn up right across the Iranian and Indo-Aryan languages. That is the first bridge from Persian towards Hindi and Urdu — not something to study now, just a reason this tiny word may feel oddly familiar when you meet those languages later.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Change only the answer, and keep everything else the same:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bale} — yes
  \item \textbf{\fa{نه}} — \emph{na} — no
\end{itemize}

Ask yourself a harmless yes/no question and answer it both ways. The two written forms stand side by side at the end of the chapter, where every model is on the page at once.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair, twice — \emph{bale} … \emph{na}
  \item which of the chapter's four words is not a loan from Arabic — \emph{na}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Answer “no” in Persian. (\emph{\textbf{Na.}}) Which of this chapter's words came from somewhere other than Arabic, and where from? (\emph{\textbf{na}} — \textbf{an old Indo-Iranian negative}.) Now say the whole chain once: \textbf{hello, thank you, yes, no.}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 1 — one tiny exchange, one tiny mark}

\label{lesson:FA-C01-practice}



\begin{quote}
Keep every model visible. Say \textbf{\fa{سلام}} once to greet and once to answer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Read each Persian line from right to left:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item A: \textbf{\fa{سلام}} — \emph{salâm}
  \item B: \textbf{\fa{سلام}} — \emph{salâm}
  \item A: \textbf{\fa{ممنون}} — \emph{mamnun}
  \item B: \textbf{\fa{بله}} or \textbf{\fa{نه}} — \emph{bale} or \emph{na}
\end{itemize}

The later three words remain visible whole-word supports. Today you are proving the greeting and the page direction, not decoding every letter.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the four-line exchange, choosing \textbf{bale} or \textbf{na}
  \item \emph{Point to:} to the right edge where each Persian line begins
  \item \emph{Copy:} \textbf{\fa{ا}} once beside the visible model, top to bottom
  \item \emph{Say it:} the old idea behind \textbf{salâm} — \textquotedblleft{}peace\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Greet once without help. Then compare your \textbf{\fa{ا}} with the model. No hidden-word spelling and no second letter: the chapter closes with one usable exchange and one supported stroke.
\end{tcolorbox}
